title: Structs, Enums and Namespaces
objectives: Define structs that group related data, construct them with brace initialisation and access members with . and ->
Use scoped enum class types for closed sets of values and explain why they beat plain enums
Organise code into namespaces and resolve name collisions
Model a price/order domain using exact integer-cents arithmetic
motivation: A fill is not one number, it is symbol, side, price, quantity, venue, timestamp. C++ lets you bind those into a struct so functions pass one coherent Order instead of six loose variables, while enum class pins 'side' to exactly Buy or Sell. Namespaces then keep your Order from colliding with a vendor library's Order. These three features are the core vocabulary of every real trading codebase.

blocks.caption: Struct layout rules the compiler follows: order fields differently, pay a different size.

blocks.md: A **struct** is a user-defined type bundling named members. Define the type once, then construct objects with **brace initialisation**, listing values in member order, nested members can be initialised with their own braces (`{"AAPL", {19050}, 100, 'B'}`). Access members with the dot operator (`order.quantity`) and, through a pointer, the arrow operator (`ptr->quantity`, shorthand for `(*ptr).quantity`). Structs make function signatures honest: `void clip(const Order& o)` cannot confuse a price with a quantity, and adding a field later updates one definition instead of a dozen parameter lists. Note the money discipline from lesson 2 built right in: `Price` stores **cents in a long long**, so every notional computed from it is exact.

blocks.caption: Brace initialisation fills members in order; the nested Price gets its own braces. Output: AAPL 1905000

blocks.text: enum class: closed sets of values

blocks.md: A **scoped enum** declares a closed set of named constants with its own type: `enum class Side { Buy, Sell };`. Compared with old-style (unscoped) enums it fixes two real problems. First, its names are *scoped*, you write `Side::Buy`, and two enums may each define `Buy` without colliding. Second, its values do **not** implicitly convert to int: `int x = Side::Buy;` is a compile error; you must write `static_cast<int>(Side::Buy)`. That friction is the point, a Side can no longer be mistaken for a share count. You can pin the underlying storage with `enum class Venue : unsigned char { Nyse, Nasdaq, Dark };`, making each venue one byte in a struct that holds millions of orders.

blocks.caption: Scoped enums compare only against their own type; the cast makes the underlying number explicit. Output: buy then 1

blocks.text: namespaces: your names versus everyone else's

blocks.md: **Namespaces** partition the global name space: `namespace risk { ... }` wraps declarations so callers write `risk::withinLimit(...)`. Two libraries can each define an `Order` because each lives in its own namespace. Prefer explicit qualification, or a targeted **using declaration** (`using risk::withinLimit;`), over the blanket `using namespace risk;` - and never put a using directive in a header, where it leaks into every includer. Namespaces are open: the same namespace can be reopened across files, which is how a library splits its implementation among source files while presenting one interface.

blocks.caption: Digit separators (1'000'000) make large constants readable; bool prints as 1/0 by default. Output: 0 then 1

blocks.text: Putting it together: a validated order

blocks.caption: One namespace holds the domain types; the risk check takes const Order&, no copy, no ambiguity. Output: 1

blocks.md: User-defined types are how a codebase stops arguing. When `Side`, `OrderId` and `Price` are distinct types, not `int`, `int` and `double` wearing comments, the compiler enforces the vocabulary the desk already uses. This is the difference between type systems as bureaucracy and type systems as free unit tests: every accidental swap of an order id and a quantity becomes a compile error instead of a 3am page.

blocks.caption: Strong types: distinct vocabularies for concepts the desk keeps distinct.

blocks.md: Three design rules worth internalising. **Scoped enums (`enum class`) always**, plain enums leak their enumerators into the enclosing scope and convert to integers implicitly, which is two bugs per keystroke saved. **Constructors of strong types get `explicit`**, it stops `f(42)` from silently becoming an `OrderId`, and makes the intended construction `OrderId{42}` visible at the call site. **Namespaces mirror ownership, not taxonomies**, `md::` (market data), `oms::` (order management), `risk::` boundaries are where build-time dependencies can be cut; a namespace named `utils::` is where good intentions go to die.

blocks.title: Why price is an integer in the example
blocks.md: Money and prices as `double` accumulate binary representation error (the numerical-stability lesson at micro scale). The professional pattern is integer ticks + a per-instrument decimal scale, exactly as the example shows, with the conversion to double confined to display and analytics boundaries. When you see `int64_t ticks` in a codebase, that team has been burned before; when you see `double price` in an order path, they will be.

blocks.title: The model is the documentation
blocks.md: Notice what this tiny model encodes: prices are exact integer cents, Side and Venue are closed sets, the risk rule is one named function. Six months from now, a new hire can read these types and understand the desk's invariants without reading a word of prose.

guidedExercise.prompt: Given `struct Price { long long cents; };` and `struct Order { std::string symbol; Price limit; int quantity; };`, write a function `long long notionalCents(const Order& o)` and print the notional for `Order{"TSLA", {24850}, 50}`. What is the exact output, and what is the notional in dollars?
hints: Multiply cents by quantity: the result stays in cents.

independentExercise.prompt: Model two candidate orders and pick the larger notional. Order A: "TSLA", limit 24850 cents, quantity 50, Side::Buy. Order B: "AAPL", limit 19050 cents, quantity 100, Side::Sell. Using an `enum class Side`, a `struct Order`, and a `namespace desk`, write a full program that prints the symbol and notional in cents of the larger order. State the exact output.
hints: Write notionalCents(const Order&) once and compare the two results; bind the winner to a reference.

commonMistakes: Accessing members of a pointer with dot syntax (o.quantity instead of o->quantity), dot is for objects and references.
Expecting enum class values to convert to int implicitly: static_cast is required, and that strictness is a feature, not an obstacle.
Putting using namespace std; in a header, it forces every includer to inherit the collisions.
Storing a price as double inside a struct 'because it is easier': use long long cents for ledger-exact money.
Defining a struct type inside a .cpp when multiple files need it: struct definitions belong in headers (with include guards).
realWorldApplication: Exchange gateway SDKs are struct-and-enum libraries: fixed order structs, scoped venue enums, and vendor namespaces you must qualify, reading those headers is a daily task on the desk.
quantFinanceApplication: The Order/Price model here, integer-cents prices, scoped Side and Venue enums, a namespace with a notional risk cap, is a miniature of a real order-management system's core types.
summary: structs bundle related members and make function signatures type-safe; construct with braces, access with . (object/reference) or -> (pointer).
enum class creates scoped, strongly-typed value sets: no name leakage and no implicit conversion to int.
Namespaces partition names; qualify explicitly or use targeted using declarations, never a using directive in a header.
Money belongs in integer cents (long long) inside structs so notionals and PnL are exact.
const-reference parameters (const Order&) pass structs without copying, the default for read-only inputs.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: 19050 cents x 100 = 1,905,000, printed without separators. Integer arithmetic on cents is exact, the whole point of the Price struct.

quiz.prompt: What does enum class add over a plain (unscoped) enum?
options: Scoped names and no implicit conversion to int
quiz.explanation: Scoped enums keep enumerators inside the enum's name (Side::Buy) and refuse implicit int conversions, accidentally mixing a Side with a share count becomes a compile error.

quiz.prompt: Given `Order* o = ⩝` where Order has a member quantity, which expression correctly reads it?
quiz.explanation: Through a pointer, use the arrow: o->quantity is shorthand for (*o).quantity. o.quantity does not compile because o is not an object or reference.

options: A targeted using declaration, e.g. using risk::withinLimit;
A using directive in a header, e.g. using namespace std;
Reopening the same namespace across several .cpp files
quiz.explanation: Explicit qualification and targeted using declarations keep dependencies visible; a using directive in a header leaks into every includer. Reopening namespaces across files is standard library organisation.

quiz.prompt: An order has limit 25750 cents and quantity 400. What is its notional in cents?
quiz.explanation: 25750 x 400 = 10,300,000 cents, i.e. \$103,000.00, exact because everything stayed in integer cents.

quiz.prompt: In `struct Price { long long cents; };`, why is the field long long rather than double?
quiz.modelAnswer: Cents are integers and long long arithmetic is exact; doubles cannot represent most decimal prices exactly (they are binary fractions), so a ledger of double prices accumulates representation error such as 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004.
quiz.explanation: Struct fields should carry the semantics you want: exactness for money, which integer cents give and binary doubles cannot.

flashcards.back: A user-defined type bundling named members; construct with brace initialisation, access with . (object/reference) or -> (pointer).
A scoped, strongly-typed enum: enumerators live inside the enum's name (Side::Buy) and never implicitly convert to int.
o.member for objects and references; ptr->member for pointers, shorthand for (*ptr).member.
Qualify explicitly or use targeted using declarations; never a using directive in a header; namespaces may be reopened across files.

flashcards.front: Price p{19050}; int qty{100};: what does p.cents * qty print?
flashcards.back: 1905000, integer cents times quantity stays exact (and prints without separators).
